specStatements.text: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but cannot be created or destroyed.
Students should be able to describe with examples where there are energy transfers in a closed system, that there is no net change to the total energy.
Students should be able to describe, with examples, how in all system changes energy is dissipated, so that it is stored in less useful ways. This energy is often described as being ‘wasted’.
Students should be able to explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers, for example through lubrication and the use of thermal insulation.
The higher the thermal conductivity of a material the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.
Students should be able to describe how the rate of cooling of a building is affected by the thickness and thermal conductivity of its walls.
Students do not need to know the definition of thermal conductivity.

Required practical activity 2 (physics only): investigate the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators and the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer)

(HT only) Students should be able to describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the definition of thermal conductivity.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Thermal conductivity is treated only as the comparative property the specification states: the higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it. No formal definition is given, no unit is quoted, and no item asks students to calculate a value of thermal conductivity or to use it in an equation. Every question about conductivity asks only which material conducts energy at the higher rate, or how conductivity and thickness together affect the rate of cooling of a building.

concepts.definition: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed. Energy that appears to have been 'lost' has always been transferred into some other store.
An energy transfer that does the job the device was designed to do, for example a lamp transferring energy to the surroundings by light, or a motor transferring energy to the kinetic store of a load.
A system in which no energy is transferred in or out. Energy may be transferred between stores inside the system, but there is no net change to the total energy of the system.
The spreading out of energy into stores that are less useful, usually the thermal store of the surroundings. In all system changes some energy is dissipated in this way.
Energy that has been dissipated and is now stored in less useful ways. It has not been destroyed, but it has spread out into the surroundings and is very difficult to use again.
Putting a lubricant such as oil between surfaces that rub together. This reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings as the parts move.
Surrounding an object or building with a material of low thermal conductivity, such as loft insulation or cavity wall insulation, so that energy is transferred out of it by conduction more slowly.

A property of a material that determines how readily energy is conducted through it. The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material. The formal definition is not required.

concepts.term: Rate of energy transfer by conduction
concepts.definition: How much energy is transferred by conduction across a material each second. Metals have high thermal conductivity and so conduct energy at a high rate; materials such as wool, foam and trapped air have low thermal conductivity and conduct at a low rate.

concepts.term: Rate of cooling of a building
concepts.definition: How quickly a building loses energy to the colder surroundings. It depends on the thickness of the walls and on their thermal conductivity: thicker walls, and walls made of a material of lower thermal conductivity, both give a lower rate of cooling.

An investigation of the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators, and of the factors that may affect the thermal insulation properties of a material. A typical method places equal volumes of hot water in identical beakers, each wrapped in a different material, and records the temperature of the water at the start and after a fixed time.

concepts.term: Control variables in the insulation investigation
concepts.definition: To make the comparison valid, the volume of water, its starting temperature, the beaker, the use of a lid and the cooling time must be the same for every material. Only the insulating material (or, in the second part, its thickness or number of layers) is changed.

Judged from the temperature change of the water over the fixed time. The smaller the temperature drop, the more effective the material is as a thermal insulator. Increasing the thickness, or the number of layers, of a material improves its insulating effect.

concepts.term: AT 1 and AT 5 in this practical
concepts.definition: AT 1 is met by using apparatus to make and record measurements accurately, here the temperature of the water with a thermometer, the volume with a measuring cylinder and the time with a stopclock. AT 5 is met by the safe use of apparatus to measure energy transfers, here the cooling of hot water through different insulating materials.

concepts.term: Working scientifically and maths skills in this practical
concepts.definition: The investigation gives opportunities to identify and control variables, to repeat readings and identify anomalies, to calculate temperature changes and mean values, and to plot and interpret graphs of temperature against time or against thickness of insulation.

The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer). Efficiency is a ratio, so it has no unit; it may be written as a decimal or as a percentage, and it can never be greater than 1 (100%).

concepts.term: Useful output and total input energy transfer
concepts.definition: The total input energy transfer is all of the energy supplied to a device. The useful output energy transfer is the part of it transferred by the intended, useful pathway; the rest has been dissipated and is described as wasted.

Efficiency may also be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input). Because power is energy transferred per second, this gives the same value as the energy equation for the same device.

The efficiency of an intended energy transfer is increased by reducing the energy dissipated in unwanted ways: lubricating moving parts to reduce friction, insulating or lagging to reduce the energy conducted away, streamlining to reduce air resistance, and choosing components that waste less, such as a lamp that heats its surroundings less.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the energy in a device as it runs?
misconceptions.correct: The total energy stays the same; it is transferred between stores, and some of it is dissipated into less useful stores.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy gets used up as a device runs, so there is less energy in total than there was at the start.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language says a battery is 'used up' or 'runs out of energy', and the useful effect really does stop, so the energy seems to have gone.
misconceptions.correction: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. When a battery goes flat its chemical store has emptied, but the same total energy is now spread through the surroundings, mostly in thermal stores.

misconceptions.question: What happens to wasted energy?
misconceptions.correct: It is dissipated: it is still there, but it is now stored in less useful ways, usually in the thermal store of the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Wasted energy is destroyed, because once it has spread into the surroundings it has gone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'wasted' suggests something thrown away, and dissipated energy cannot be recovered in practice, so students treat it as no longer existing.
misconceptions.correction: Energy cannot be destroyed. Wasted energy has only been dissipated, so it is stored less usefully and is spread too thinly to be transferred back.

misconceptions.question: How does the total energy of a closed system change while energy is transferred inside it?
misconceptions.correct: There is no net change to the total energy of a closed system, however many transfers happen inside it.
misconceptions.misconception: Some energy always leaks out of the system when parts rub, so the total energy of a closed system falls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that friction dissipates energy, then assume the dissipated energy has left the system, forgetting that in a closed system it is still inside.
misconceptions.correction: In a closed system no energy is transferred in or out. Friction moves energy into thermal stores inside the system, so the total is unchanged even though the useful stores empty.

misconceptions.question: Can dissipated energy be collected and used again?
misconceptions.correct: In practice no, because it has spread out into the surroundings and is stored far too thinly to be transferred back usefully.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy dissipated to the surroundings is stored there and will come back to the device later, so nothing is really lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are told energy is never destroyed and conclude that it must therefore still be available for use.
misconceptions.correction: Conservation says the energy still exists, not that it is still useful. Once it is dissipated it is stored in less useful ways and cannot be recovered by the device.

misconceptions.question: What does lubricating a machine do to friction?
misconceptions.correct: It reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated as the surfaces move over one another.
misconceptions.misconception: Oil removes friction completely, so a lubricated machine dissipates no energy at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lubricated parts feel effortless to turn, and textbooks say oil is used 'to stop friction', which sounds absolute.
misconceptions.correction: Lubrication lowers friction but never removes it. Some energy is still dissipated, which is why in all system changes some energy is stored in less useful ways.

misconceptions.question: What does thermal insulation do to the energy transferred out of a building?
misconceptions.correct: It reduces the rate at which energy is transferred out by conduction, so the building cools more slowly.
misconceptions.misconception: Insulation stops energy escaping altogether, so an insulated building does not cool down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Insulation is described as 'keeping the heat in', which sounds like a complete barrier rather than a slowing down.
misconceptions.correction: Insulating materials have a low thermal conductivity, so energy is still conducted out, just at a lower rate. The building still cools, only more slowly.

misconceptions.question: Does insulating material make a room warmer?
misconceptions.correct: No. It does not supply any energy; it only slows the rate at which energy is transferred out of the room.
misconceptions.misconception: Insulation generates warmth of its own and adds it to the room, which is why insulated rooms feel warmer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Advertising talks about materials that 'keep you warm', and a coat feels warm, so the material seems to be the source of the energy.
misconceptions.correction: No energy can be created. A coat or a layer of loft insulation only reduces the rate of transfer away from the warm object inside it.

misconceptions.question: Is a material with a high thermal conductivity a good insulator?
misconceptions.correct: No. The higher the thermal conductivity, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction, so it is a good conductor and a poor insulator.
misconceptions.misconception: A high thermal conductivity means the material is good at holding energy in, so it insulates well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'High' is read as 'better', and the words conductivity and insulation are not clearly separated in students' minds.
misconceptions.correction: High thermal conductivity means energy passes across the material quickly. Good insulators are the materials with low thermal conductivity.

misconceptions.question: Does making a wall thicker change the thermal conductivity of the brick?
misconceptions.correct: No. Thermal conductivity is a property of the material itself; thickness is a separate factor that also affects the rate of cooling.
misconceptions.misconception: Thicker material has a lower thermal conductivity, which is why thick walls keep a building warm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both thickness and conductivity affect the rate of cooling, so students merge the two into a single idea.
misconceptions.correction: The brick has the same thermal conductivity however thick the wall is. The rate of cooling is lower because the energy has further to be conducted, not because the material has changed.

misconceptions.question: How does the thickness of a building's walls affect its rate of cooling?
misconceptions.correct: Thicker walls give a lower rate of cooling, because energy is transferred by conduction across them more slowly.
misconceptions.misconception: Thicker walls cool a building faster, because there is more material for the energy to move through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of more material as more pathways for energy, rather than as a greater distance for the energy to be conducted across.
misconceptions.correction: More thickness means energy must be conducted further, which lowers the rate of transfer. A thicker wall of the same material always cools the building more slowly.

misconceptions.question: In the insulation practical, which material is the best insulator?
misconceptions.correct: The one with the smallest temperature drop over the fixed time, since least energy has been transferred out of the water.
misconceptions.misconception: The best insulator is the one whose water changed temperature the most, because that shows the material was doing the most work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for the biggest number in the results table and treat 'largest change' as 'best performance'.
misconceptions.correction: The purpose of the insulator is to reduce the energy transferred out, so the best material is the one that leaves the water hottest, with the smallest temperature change.

misconceptions.question: Which temperature readings does the insulation investigation need?
misconceptions.correct: The temperature at the start and at the end of a measured time, so that the temperature change can be calculated, with repeats.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the final temperature needs to be recorded, because that is the reading the insulating material affects.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In a well-controlled test all the beakers start at the same temperature, so the starting reading feels like something already known rather than something measured.
misconceptions.correction: The temperature change is what is being compared, so both readings are needed, and repeats are needed before a mean can be calculated.

misconceptions.question: What must be kept the same when different insulating materials are compared?
misconceptions.correct: The volume and starting temperature of the water, the beaker and lid, and the time the water is left to cool.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the material needs to be changed and nothing else matters, because the material is what is being tested.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'change one thing' but not the second half of the rule, that everything else must be deliberately held constant.
misconceptions.correction: Changing one variable is only valid if all other variables that affect cooling are controlled. Different volumes or starting temperatures would make the comparison meaningless.

misconceptions.question: How is efficiency calculated from energy transfers?
misconceptions.correct: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer)
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency is the total input energy transfer divided by the useful output energy transfer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the equation is a fraction of two energies but not which is on top, and dividing the bigger number by the smaller feels more natural.
misconceptions.correction: The useful output goes on top. Writing it the other way round gives a value greater than 1 for any real device, which is a clear sign the fraction has been inverted.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of efficiency?
misconceptions.correct: Efficiency has no unit. It is a ratio of two energy transfers, or of two powers, so the units cancel.
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency is measured in joules when energies are used, and in watts when powers are used.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities in the equation carry a unit, so students attach that unit to the answer instead of cancelling it.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing joules by joules, or watts by watts, leaves a pure number. Efficiency is written as a decimal or as a percentage, never with a unit.

misconceptions.question: What does the value of efficiency tell you?
misconceptions.correct: It tells you the fraction of the total input that is transferred usefully.
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency tells you the fraction of the input energy that is wasted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lessons on efficiency concentrate on wasted energy, so students associate the number with waste rather than with useful output.
misconceptions.correction: The useful output is on top of the fraction, so efficiency is the useful share. The wasted share is what is left when the efficiency is taken away from 1 (or 100%).

misconceptions.question: Can the efficiency of a device be greater than 1?
misconceptions.correct: No. The useful output energy transfer can never exceed the total input energy transfer, so efficiency is at most 1 (100%).
misconceptions.misconception: A very good device can have an efficiency above 1, because it produces more than it is given.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Inverting the equation, or dividing input by output, produces numbers such as 1.67, and students accept them without checking against conservation of energy.
misconceptions.correction: Energy cannot be created, so the useful output is always part of the input. Any efficiency above 1 means the fraction has been written upside down.

misconceptions.question: Does supplying a device with more energy make it more efficient?
misconceptions.correct: No. Efficiency is a ratio, so increasing the input raises the wasted energy in the same proportion unless the unwanted transfers are reduced.
misconceptions.misconception: You increase efficiency by supplying more power, because the device then does more work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More efficient' is used in everyday speech to mean 'gets more done', so students think about total output rather than the ratio.
misconceptions.correction: Efficiency only rises if a larger share of the input is transferred usefully, which means reducing the energy dissipated in unwanted ways.

misconceptions.question: Can a machine be made 100% efficient?
misconceptions.correct: No. In all system changes some energy is dissipated, so some of the input is always stored in less useful ways.
misconceptions.misconception: A machine that is oiled and insulated well enough wastes nothing and becomes 100% efficient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that lubrication and insulation reduce unwanted transfers and extend 'reduce' to 'eliminate'.
misconceptions.correction: These measures lower the energy dissipated but cannot remove it. Efficiency can be raised towards 1 but never reaches it for a real machine.

misconceptions.question: Should the final temperature be a control variable in the insulation practical?
misconceptions.correct: No. The final temperature is the outcome being measured, so it is the dependent variable, not something held the same.
misconceptions.misconception: To be fair, every material should be made to finish at the same temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that a fair test keeps things the same and apply the rule to every quantity in the table, including the measured result.
misconceptions.correction: Only the variables that could affect the result are controlled. The final temperature is what the different materials are expected to change, so it must be free to vary.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about energy is correct?

options.text: Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but never created.
options.rationale: This is the conservation statement: energy can move between stores and be dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed.

options.text: Energy is gradually used up as a device runs, so the total slowly falls.
options.rationale: Students who think a battery 'runs out of energy' believe the total amount decreases rather than being transferred away.

options.text: Energy that is wasted is destroyed once it spreads into the surroundings.
options.rationale: Wasted energy cannot be recovered, so students conclude that it no longer exists.

options.text: Energy can be created inside a device as long as fuel is supplied to it.
options.rationale: Students treat fuel as a source that makes new energy rather than as a chemical store that is emptied.

mcqs.stem: A wind-up toy is treated as a closed system. As it runs down, what happens to the total energy of the system?

options.text: It falls steadily, because energy escapes as the moving parts rub together.
options.rationale: Students know friction dissipates energy and assume the dissipated energy has left the system.

options.text: It stays the same, because energy is transferred between stores inside it.
options.rationale: In a closed system no energy enters or leaves, so there is no net change to the total energy however many transfers occur.

options.text: It falls to zero, because the stored energy is used up by the moving parts.
options.rationale: The toy stops, so students conclude the energy has been consumed rather than dissipated inside the system.

options.text: It rises a little, because the friction between the moving parts makes energy.
options.rationale: Students who see warming as energy appearing treat friction as a source of new energy.

mcqs.stem: An electric drill becomes warm while it is being used. What has happened to the energy that warmed it?

options.text: It has been destroyed, because warming the surroundings is not a useful result.
options.rationale: Students equate 'not useful' with 'gone', so they treat wasted energy as destroyed.

options.text: It is stored in the drill and will be transferred back usefully as it cools.
options.rationale: Students told energy is never destroyed assume dissipated energy remains available for use.

options.text: It has been dissipated, and is now stored less usefully in the surroundings.
options.rationale: Energy transferred by friction inside the drill spreads into thermal stores of the drill and the air, where it is stored in a less useful way.

options.text: It has been transferred usefully, because a warm drill cuts through wood faster.
options.rationale: Students look for a purpose for every transfer and invent one rather than call the transfer wasteful.

mcqs.stem: Why does oiling the moving parts of a machine reduce unwanted energy transfers?

options.text: It removes friction entirely, so the machine dissipates no energy as it runs.
options.rationale: Oiled parts turn very easily, so students believe friction has been eliminated rather than reduced.

options.text: It insulates the parts, so all of the energy is kept inside the machine itself.
options.rationale: Students merge the two named methods and think oil acts as a barrier that stops all transfer.

options.text: It adds energy to the moving parts, so the machine needs less from the supply.
options.rationale: Students who think a treatment can supply energy see the oil as an extra source.

options.text: It reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal store around it.
options.rationale: Lubrication lowers the friction between surfaces that rub, so less of the input energy is transferred to thermal stores.

mcqs.stem: A cold loft is lined with a thick layer of mineral wool. Why does this reduce unwanted energy transfers from the house?

options.text: Mineral wool has a low thermal conductivity, so energy is conducted away slower.
options.rationale: A material of low thermal conductivity gives a low rate of energy transfer by conduction, so the house cools more slowly.

options.text: Mineral wool generates extra warmth, which it adds to the rooms below the loft.
options.rationale: Insulation is described as 'keeping you warm', so students treat it as a source of energy.

options.text: Mineral wool stops the transfer completely, so the house can no longer cool down.
options.rationale: Students read insulation as a total barrier rather than as something that lowers the rate.

options.text: Mineral wool stores the wasted energy until the rooms below the loft need it.
options.rationale: Students who know energy is conserved assume dissipated energy is being saved for later use.

mcqs.stem: Two slabs of the same thickness, one copper and one brick, separate a warm room from the cold air outside. Copper has the higher thermal conductivity. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Energy crosses the brick slab faster, because copper is the better insulator.
options.rationale: Students who read 'high conductivity' as 'good at holding energy in' reverse the relationship.

options.text: Energy is transferred by conduction across the copper slab at the higher rate.
options.rationale: The higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across it.

options.text: The two rates are equal, because the slabs have exactly the same thickness.
options.rationale: Students who confuse thickness with conductivity think equal thickness must mean equal rates.

options.text: Energy crosses each slab at a rate set only by the temperature of the room.
options.rationale: Students recall that a temperature difference drives conduction and conclude the material makes no difference.

mcqs.stem: A saucepan needs a base that transfers energy quickly to the food and a handle that stays cool enough to hold. Which choice of materials best achieves this?

options.text: A base of low thermal conductivity and a handle of high thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: Students who think high conductivity keeps energy in put the conducting material where it should not be.

options.text: A thick base and a thin handle, both made from the same metal alloy throughout.
options.rationale: Students who believe thickness sets conductivity try to solve the problem with dimensions alone.

options.text: A base of high thermal conductivity and a handle of low thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: The high conductivity base gives a high rate of transfer to the food; the low conductivity handle gives a low rate of transfer to the hand.

options.text: A base and a handle both of high thermal conductivity, so energy spreads evenly.
options.rationale: Students value even heating and overlook that the handle would then conduct energy to the hand.

mcqs.stem: Two houses are identical except that one has thicker external walls made of the same brick. How does the rate of cooling of the house with the thicker walls compare?

options.text: It is higher, because thicker walls hold more material for energy to move through.
options.rationale: Students picture extra material as extra pathways rather than as a greater distance.

options.text: It is lower, because making the brick thicker lowers its thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: The direction is right but the reason is wrong: conductivity is a property of the material, not of the thickness.

options.text: It is the same, because both houses are built from exactly the same kind of brick.
options.rationale: Students who focus only on the material forget that thickness is a second factor.

options.text: It is lower, because energy is conducted across the thicker walls more slowly.
options.rationale: Increasing the thickness of the walls lowers the rate of energy transfer by conduction, so the building cools more slowly.

mcqs.stem: Four designs are proposed for the external walls of the same building. Which design gives the lowest rate of cooling?

options.text: Thick walls made from a material with a low thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: Both factors act in the same direction here: greater thickness and lower conductivity each lower the rate of energy transfer by conduction.

options.text: Thick walls made from a material with a high thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: Students who read high conductivity as good insulation choose the conducting material.

options.text: Thin walls made from a material with a low thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: Students who think thick walls cool a building faster pick the thin option.

options.text: Thin walls made from a material with a high thermal conductivity.
options.rationale: Students who reverse both factors at once choose the design that actually cools fastest.

mcqs.stem: Equal volumes of water at 80 °C are put in four identical beakers, each wrapped in a different material. After 10 minutes the temperatures are P 62 °C, Q 55 °C, R 71 °C and S 48 °C. Which material is the most effective insulator?

options.text: S, because the water it wrapped showed by far the largest temperature change of all.
options.rationale: Students pick the biggest number in the table and read a large change as good performance.

options.text: R, because the water it wrapped fell through the smallest temperature change.
options.rationale: The smallest temperature drop, 9 °C, shows that least energy was transferred out of that beaker, so R is the best insulator.

options.text: None of them, because a good insulator would have kept the water at exactly 80 °C.
options.rationale: Students who think insulation stops all energy transfer reject every result as a failure.

options.text: P, because its final temperature is closest to the middle of the four results.
options.rationale: Students who look for a typical or average value choose the middle result rather than the extreme one.

mcqs.stem: In this investigation, which quantities must be kept the same for every material tested?

options.text: Only the material being tested, since nothing else has any effect on cooling.
options.rationale: Students remember 'change one thing' but not that everything else must be held constant.

options.text: The final temperature of the water, so that each material can be compared fairly.
options.rationale: Students apply 'keep it the same' to the measured outcome, confusing the dependent variable with a control.

options.text: The volume and starting temperature of the water, and the time left to cool.
options.rationale: These all affect how much the water cools, so they must be controlled if the comparison between materials is to be valid.

options.text: The thickness of the beaker glass, though the volume of water may be varied freely.
options.rationale: Students control a variable that is already fixed by using identical beakers while letting a genuine one vary.

mcqs.stem: Required practical activity 2 develops AT 1 and AT 5. Which measurements does the investigation actually require?

options.text: Only the final temperature of the water, since that is what the material changes.
options.rationale: Students treat the common starting temperature as already known rather than as a reading to be taken.

options.text: Only the volume of water, because equal volumes make the test fair on their own.
options.rationale: Students name a single control variable and assume it is sufficient for a valid comparison.

options.text: Only the room temperature, because the water cools towards the room's own value.
options.rationale: Students know the surroundings set the final temperature and mistake that for the measurement needed.

options.text: The temperature of the water at the start and at the end of a measured time.
options.rationale: AT 1 and AT 5 are met by using a thermometer and a stopclock to record the temperature change that shows how much energy has been transferred.

mcqs.stem: A student repeats the test three times for each material. For one material, one of the three readings is far from the other two. What is the best thing to do?

options.text: Identify it as anomalous, leave it out of the mean and record why it was left out.
options.rationale: Identifying anomalies and excluding them from a mean, with a reason given, is the correct handling of repeated readings.

options.text: Include it in the mean anyway, because leaving out data makes the test unfair.
options.rationale: Students treat 'fair test' as meaning every number collected must be used.

options.text: Ignore the means and just compare one final temperature for each material.
options.rationale: Students who think a single final reading is enough abandon repeats altogether.

options.text: Change the starting temperature of the water and repeat the whole test again.
options.rationale: Students respond to an odd result by altering the method rather than by examining the reading.

mcqs.stem: A lamp is supplied with 500 J of energy and transfers 40 J of it usefully by light. What is the efficiency of the lamp?

options.rationale: The fraction has been inverted: 500 / 40 = 12.5, an impossible efficiency.
efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer = 40 / 500 = 0.08.
The wasted fraction, 460 / 500, has been calculated instead of the useful fraction.
The wasted energy in joules has been found by subtraction and given as the efficiency.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the efficiency of an energy transfer is correct?

options.text: It is the total input energy transfer divided by the useful output energy transfer.
options.rationale: Students recall a fraction of two energies but put the larger quantity on top.

options.text: It is the useful output energy transfer, measured in joules for any given device.
options.rationale: Students attach the unit of the quantities in the equation to the answer instead of cancelling it.

options.text: It is the useful output energy transfer divided by the total input energy transfer.
options.rationale: This is the equation given in the specification, and it makes efficiency the useful share of the input.

options.text: It can be greater than 1 for a device whose output is larger than its input.
options.rationale: Students accept values above 1 without checking them against conservation of energy.

mcqs.stem: A motor has a total power input of 250 W and a useful power output of 150 W. What is its efficiency?

options.rationale: The fraction has been inverted: 250 / 150 = 1.67, which conservation of energy forbids.
The wasted share, 100 / 250, has been calculated instead of the useful share.
The input has been squared or a decimal point mislaid, giving 150 / 2500.
efficiency = useful power output / total power input = 150 / 250 = 0.60.

mcqs.stem: A lift motor has an efficiency of 0.45. Which change would increase the efficiency of the intended energy transfer?

options.text: Lubricating the bearings, so less energy is dissipated as the parts rub together.
options.rationale: Reducing friction reduces the energy dissipated, so a larger share of the input energy is transferred usefully.

options.text: Supplying the motor with more power, so that its useful output is larger too.
options.rationale: Students think about total output rather than the ratio, so more input looks like more efficiency.

options.text: Nothing at all, because any well-oiled motor is already fully efficient anyway.
options.rationale: Students extend 'lubrication reduces waste' to 'lubrication removes waste'.

options.rationale: Students confuse the amount of work a device does with the fraction of the input it uses usefully.

mcqs.stem: Lagging the pipes of a hot water system increases the efficiency of the intended energy transfer. Why?

options.text: The boiler is forced to supply more energy, so its useful output rises as well.
options.rationale: Students look for a bigger input rather than a bigger useful fraction of the input.

options.text: Less energy is dissipated to the surroundings, so more of the input is useful.
options.rationale: The lagging has a low thermal conductivity, so less of the input energy is conducted away and the useful share of the input rises.

options.text: The lagging removes every unwanted transfer, making the system fully efficient.
options.rationale: Students treat insulation as eliminating dissipation rather than reducing its rate.

options.text: The lagging warms the water further, raising it well above the boiler's set value.
options.rationale: Students who think insulation supplies energy expect the water to become hotter than the boiler setting.
